story_text.value:
Hello HN, just wanted to share my project that I've been working on the past months, where I noticed the issue that now we ship faster than setting up the requirements for the project. So I thought of building secureVibe to find vulnerabilities in your codebase. Now I have a MVP where it doesn't just scan the code and show random analysis I used Tree-sitter and AST to understand code context to validate vulnerabilities found as it builds a graph of application routes, handlers and database calls so it helps to determine whether findings are confirmed or likely.

Briefly the features: 1- shows all vulnerabilities in your code with code snippets

2-fixing with ai option (optional with your own api key for now)

3- ask the graph feature as you can ask where the attacker can exploit my website or authentication issues (I used graphify as foundation for it )

4- You can filter vulnerabilities categories (like Cwe, database injection and more) from dashboard and you can download it as html report simple interactive one so you can fix it on your own later.

I would love to know your thoughts and feedback to continue on the development on it like some of the problems I faced is benchmarks to validate security rules. With some research I found openssf benchmark

so would really appreciate feedback to continue on developing with next phases.

It works best with TypeScript

story_text.value:
I've made Return to Repeat, an album and a browser music player with ten songs without beginning or end. It has built-in musical variations, some you can control and interact with and some that activate based on things like date, time of day, visit counts and current moon phase. Try the birds on track three for a starting place.

Wanted to explore other ways of releasing and experiencing digital music, and perhaps finding a route back to kind of "being" with music. My last release was a cassette in an edition of three, that also came with a minimal web player.

It's built mainly with Tone.js on the Web Audio API, with help from Claude (writing code, debugging). The music is composed as (sometimes long) seamless loops, with multiple stems for variations. Didn't want to go the proper app-route, with the main trade-off being no background audio. Also had some trouble with airplay, but think I've managed to get rid of the most obvious bugs.

Love to hear what you think of the listening experience! Happy to answer any questions about the project.

story_text.value:
Hi all, I am a professor in algorithm engineering. In our field we use a method of falsifiable hypothesis testing to improve algorithms. More precisely, this is a cycle consisting of designing an algorithm, analyzing the algorithm, then implementing it and lastly testing it using experiments on real-world instances which leads to designing new algorithms based on the current observations.

We put this methodology into an AI skill which runs in an infinite loop. This skill first creates a performance profile, then produces a hypothesis which is implemented and tested automatically using an AI agent. If the change improved the performance and tests negotiated with the user verify it, the change is kept, if not it is discarded. Everything is tracked via version control.

Part of the output is a pdf report which documents all the code changes and progress over time as well as individual patches to only merge specific patches if one chooses to do so. Moreover, this comes with a knowledge-base in which we collect global optimization knowledge, thereby improving the skill over time.

We ran this on a wide range of public code bases, e.g. our KaHIP graph partitioning toolkit, which improved running time by 3.9x, or our VieCut minimum cut solver, where the skill improved the running time of the system by 8.9x; I do believe the skill is very easy to use and hence am sharing this here. Let me know what you think!

title.value: Show HN: An agent skill that optimizes code with falsifiable hypotheses

story_text.value:
We built NariQ: 3-bit-or-lower quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B that retain near-BF16 quality across agentic tasks, math, multilingual reasoning, and image understanding.

To our knowledge, this is the first 3-bit-or-lower quantization that retains BF16 lvl performance on long-horizon agentic tasks.

Benchmarks (BF16 / 3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit):

- DeepSWE: 39.8 / 41.0 / 41.9 / 28.6

- Terminal-Bench 2.1: 62.6 / 63.8 / 60.2 / 52.4

- AIME 25+26: 97.7 / 98.3 / 96.5 / 86.0

- MSGM: 94.0 / 93.1 / 91.8 / 90.6

- RealWorldQA: 82.4 / 82.4 / 81.3 / 80.9

Decode speed is comparable to other quants on an RTX PRO 6000. Context-length results below

(3-bit / 2.5-bit / 2-bit / Unsloth UD-IQ3_XXS):

- 4K: 88.9 / 99.2 / 111.7 / 94.7

- 16K: 84.5 / 93.8 / 105.1 / 89.8

- 64K: 70.7 / 77.5 / 85.0 / 74.8

Running these currently require our llama.cpp fork: (https://github.com/nari-labs/nari-llama.cpp)

Feedback and questions welcome. We'd love to hear how these perform on your workloads.

title.value: NariQ: BF16-level Qwen3.8-27B in a 10 GB file

story_text.value:
I was sick and tired of the bloated mess that Hermes Agent has become, often dealing with hard-to-triage bugs that made managing agents a part-time job. I don't need a self-improving magical agent, I need;

- A primary agent to chat to, with sub-agent delegation

- Isolated sub-agent workspaces, tools, binaries and skills

- Kanban and cron-tasks to manage tasks

- An easy way to chat (Telegram, Web UI)

I built shoebox, crazy simple filesystem-based AI agent orchestration that uses a basic folder-structure to determine which agents to run, what they should do, and what capabilities they have.

Been running this on prod-level workloads (with extended product-development runs) and have been very happy with the results.

Curious to hear what you think!

story_text.value:
I was about to keep track of my clients and prospecting in Google Sheets for my solopreneur business, when I remembered that's exactly what I advise my clients not to do.

Created Hermit CRM, an open source CRM for 1 person. Hermit helps to keep track of deals and prospecting. The platform is built for AI by storing the data in Markdown files in git, stored locally and can be accessed with a web app, CLI or MCP. No telemetry on the app. Building in public, even the website stats are public as well.

It’s macOS first. Linux is less tested, and Windows isn’t supported.

Features I'm proud of: - import somebody from LinkedIn into to the CRM with 1 click - adding a LinkedIn convo to the CRM with 1 click. Both work without LinkedIn or CRM subs.

Don't like what you see? Fork the Hermit with your AI.

Would love to learn how you're using Hermit and where it doesn't fit your workflows.

story_text.value:
I've been working in tech for around 10 years but I have absolutely no experience at all in tech recruiting. However I have had the experience (well, often displeasure) of going through tech recruiters and the tech hiring process when applying for jobs during my career.

As with probably many of you, I'm quite frustrated with how tech hiring has been in the last year or two during the AI/LLM era. It's incredibly frustrating to send tens to hundreds of CVs for applications you would be an excellent fit for and seeing the roles go to less qualified candidates, or candidates who just end up leaving after a few months or a year. This has left me wondering how tech recruiters are assessed on their recruiting skills and retaining qualified talent within their respective organizations.

For those of you who work or have worked in tech recruiting, or have insider knowledge regarding how tech recruiters are assessed, could you share some insight into how tech recruiters are assessed? Is there any kind of follow-up regarding the performance of the people have hired, retention rates, and so on?

title.value: Ask HN: How are tech recruiters assessed on their recruiting skills?

story_text.value: Math is becoming increasingly difficult, and we can see that proofs are getting so complex they will probably take more than a human lifetime to solve. Don’t worry about AI stealing the joy of discovery, we still have the joy of understanding something that exists outside the human world. AI will let us tackle problems that were impossible within a single lifespan, and maybe we will even be able to understand some of the most exotic concepts. To me, AI has alien capabilities in math, just like many mathematicians and physicists do. AI's thinking feels just as alien to me as Einstein’s thinking once did. All I can do is watch these beautiful, exotic patterns unravel in front of me, and I love the idea that I get to catch a glimpse of this.

story_text.value:
Hi HN -

This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you!

Our team shipped a benchmark: KradleBench. We test AI in Minecraft Worlds.

1. The worlds are multi-agent. Humans and other AIs are in there too, often pursuing their own goals. Collaboration and conflict skills fall out of this property.

2. The world are dynamic. They constantly change, which means that agents need to react. “Capture the Flag” has a single winning condition, and many different ways to achieve it. This leads to many emergent and creative strategies.

3. The worlds are real-time. They are not turn-based, they do not wait for AIs to finish thinking. Nature balanced speed and intelligence in humans, we can understand this in AIs too.

Underneath all this is Kradle, a platform to test and understand intelligence. It’s a petri dish where any intelligence type (LLM, World Model, Human) can be compared and generate useful information to improve current systems, whether it’s on capabilities or safety.

Some findings so far: - A skilled human was #1, until yesterday when Astra 6.2 surpassed them. We lose badly on solo tasks and out-compete on multi-agent ones - Astra 6.2 iterates on its strategy 4x faster than Fable 5.2. The Claude family tends to think hard and stick with strategies. The OpenAI models tend to be more reactive and iterative, which serves them well in multi-agent, dynamic, real-time evals.

We’ve got videos on all the top model’s page, and we’ll be producing them when a new model launches. Sign up on the site to get them and for when the platform opens.

Thanks for reading,

James & Kemal

story_text.value:
I now feel that the math world will eventually become like the programming world: responsible for all kinds of strange hypotheses and creations.

Then let AI verify them, do the work, get the results, and reinvent the wheel over and over again, but every wheel is made differently.

There are millions of ways to implement a feature, and the same goes for proving a mathematical conjecture.

I really miss the time before AI, the feeling of being immersed in writing code and the sense of achievement after completing a feature.

And being able to happily share with others the methods I found during development and my design ideas.

But now, I can only pursue features and rough design directions. It's become like having meetings with AI every day to discuss features.

But I can't go back to the old-fashioned way of programming anymore, because I can no longer purely immerse myself in writing a program.

Because I know that whatever I write, AI can do it in a few seconds, and do it better. I can't get any sense of achievement, and the time I spend becomes purely a waste of time.

I've already given up now. I'm not some top student from a top university, or some top talent who has worked at a top company.

The ambition I used to have is gone. All that's left is the thought of "destroy everything together, then create completely new rules and a new world."

story_text.value:
I built Smartesto (for iOS, iPadOS, macOS) because I wanted a quick way to run predefined prompts (I call them actions) on a webpage or selected text, using the Share Sheet or Shortcuts. For example "Summarize a webpage", "Proofread" selected text, "Improve text", etc.

Depending on the action, I wanted to send the text to different AI providers via their APIs or process it locally on my device. And it does just that.

It works with APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral, Gemini, as well as Apple’s on-device models (using local text processing).

I also ran into pages that AI providers couldn’t access because they blocked AI bots. To address that, I built a custom Readability package that quickly extracts the page text on the device. Smartesto then passes the extracted text to the selected action for processing.

You can find the download, screenshots and videos here: https://www.giuliomagnifico.dev/apps/smartesto/

If you have similar needs, give it a try and see if it works for you (and I’d appreciate your feedback)

story_text.value:
In short:

For the past few years, I've been building a biohacking platform called Plants Research Pro (PRP), designed to help people discover research on bioactive materials and put that research to practical use. Recently, I added a new feature to PRP which is turning out to be my favorite so far: The Chess Lab. This is essentially a set of tools and protocols for biohacking in chess, some of which you can try right now via the link -- I recommend a Single-Session Experiment, which is a 6-test protocol that lets you explore how some intervention, like coffee, might improve your cognitive function in the context of chess.

-

In detail:

The idea for Chess Lab started about four years ago when I came across research by Prof. David O. Kennedy's group showing that sage, cocoa, and other materials can enhance some cognitive functions. If I remember correctly, the subjects were healthy young adults (possibly uni students). I really wanted to test this on myself, and since I like chess, I chose chess as my 'test platform'. I'm not gonna go into the formulation, but I tried sage alone, sage with cocoa, and sage with cocoa and milk. The third mix seemed to give me the best focus and attention (for about 4-6 h), and my rating started to climb after a few weeks. But there was an issue - I had no idea if I was simply improving naturally, or if the mixture was enhancing it. This annoyed me a little bit, and made me realize that PRP needed an N-of-1 experimentation system.

After finally getting around to it, PRP's Experiments system was implemented earlier this year, while Chess Lab was added about a month ago. Both are now live, although testing and refinement are ongoing. The system also supports N>1 experiments, so can be used with a group of people as well.

There are six cognitive tests and a Single-Session Experiment (SSE) to play with for free. The tests are based on those used in cognitive research, while SSE is a simple before-and-after experiment. i.e., you choose an intervention (coffee, tea, exercise, etc.), complete 6 baseline cognitive tests, apply the intervention (drink your coffee or whatever), then repeat the tests to see what changed -- all within a day (or about 1 h for simple SSEs). The results are exploratory, of course, but I think it's pretty cool that I can now do this myself, at home, without going to a university lab.

But I want to make it much better. The signal-to-noise ratio is difficult to estimate, and there are several sources of error. For instance, a chessboard recall test uses positions from real games, but some pawn structures are much easier to memorize than others. I'm examining two approaches: (1) filtering games by board complexity, and (2) introducing random configurations. The thing with (2), though, is that it's less fun and measures a somewhat different aspect of cognition, but that's a story for another day.

For longer experiments, I've added Chess.com statistics, including move accuracy, rating, opponent-adjusted score, etc. And if you're not sure how to set it up, you can describe what you want in plain language (e.g., 'I want to test if lemon peel can improve my chess') and an AI-powered builder will create a research-backed recipe, design the experiment, assign metrics, and select suitable cognitive tests. AI can also help interpret the statistical results. These full experiments are part of the Premium subscription.

In the coming months, I'll add more cognitive tests, analytics, and some ML capability. Most importantly, I hope to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. A new Multi-Session Crossover design (repeated SSEs alternating intervention/no-intervention days, with longitudinal analysis) should help, but there'll definitely be more work needed from different angles.

Anyway, if you like chess and the idea of (safely) optimizing cognitive performance with biohacking, give Chess Lab a try! I'd be very keen for feedback, bug reports, or feature suggestions. Thanks!
